summary: DHCPv6 prefix delegation lets a router hand a block of IPv6 addresses to another router. This RFC adds an option that lets the delegating side exclude one specific sub-prefix from the block it hands out, for example one already in use on the link between the two routers. It updates RFC 3633.

plainLanguage.summary: When one router hands a block of IPv6 addresses to another, the rules say it cannot use any of that block itself. That leaves the network with two routes for the same customer: one for the link between the routers and one for the customer site. This RFC lets the handing-over router keep one prefix out of the block for its own link, by naming it in a new DHCPv6 option. The router that receives the block must then leave that prefix alone.

questions: how to exclude a prefix in dhcpv6 prefix delegation
what is dhcpv6 option pd exclude
how does dhcpv6 prefix delegation exclude a prefix
subtitle: Lets a DHCPv6 server carve one prefix out of a delegated block, such as the one already used on the link.

tldr.problem: The rules for DHCPv6 prefix delegation say that a delegated prefix cannot be used by the delegating router. A network that wants a single aggregated route for a customer, rather than one route for the link between the routers and another for the customer site, cannot use that prefix for the link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a DHCPv6 option, code 67, that appears inside the delegated prefix option and names exactly one prefix to be excluded from the block. The delegating router uses that prefix on its own link to the requesting router, and the requesting router must not put it on any of its downstream interfaces.
tldr.outcome: The customer can be represented by one aggregated prefix while the link keeps its own prefix, and the excluded prefix is still part of the delegated block. The option is optional, and a router that does not use it falls back to the normal behaviour.

today: RFC 6603 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2012, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes it. It updates RFC 3633, which is the prefix delegation specification it extends.

sections.title: What the Option Is For
sections.content:
The RFC defines an optional mechanism and the related DHCPv6 option that allow one specific prefix to be excluded from a delegated prefix set when DHCPv6-based prefix delegation is used.

The mechanism targets deployments where prefix delegation is used but a single aggregated route or prefix has to represent one customer, instead of one prefix for the link between the delegating router and the requesting router and another for the customer network behind it. It lets the delegating router use a prefix out of the delegated prefix set on the link through which it exchanges DHCPv6 messages with the requesting router. It is intended for networks where each requesting router is on its own layer 2 domain.
sections.plainLanguage:
Some networks want a single route that covers the whole customer, rather than two routes: one for the link between the routers and one for the site behind them. The rule that stops the handing-over router from using any of the delegated block is what forces the second route.

This RFC lets the handing-over router keep one prefix out of the block for its own link, and it is meant for networks where each customer router sits on its own local network segment.

sections.title: The Problem the Rule Causes
sections.content:
DHCPv6 prefix delegation, defined in RFC 3633, has an explicit limitation: a prefix delegated to a requesting router cannot be used by the delegating router. The delegating router therefore ends up with two routes towards a customer that cannot be aggregated, one for the link between the requesting router and the delegating router and one for the customer site behind the requesting router.

There are architectures and link models where a host, for example a mobile router that is also acting as a requesting router, always has a single /64 prefix configured on its uplink interface, and the delegating router is also the requesting router's first-hop router. It may also be required that the prefix configured on the uplink interface has to be aggregatable with the delegated prefixes. That combination creates a problem for DHCPv6 prefix delegation together with stateless (RFC 4862) or stateful (RFC 3315) address autoconfiguration on a link where the /64 that is advertised is also part of the prefix delegated to the requesting router, for example a /56.
sections.plainLanguage:
The rule exists because the block of addresses is meant to belong entirely to the customer. Because of it, the network carries two routes towards that customer, and the two cannot be combined into one.

The problem appears on mobile and other single-homed routers, which always have one prefix on the link to the provider and take their addresses from the provider's router. There the prefix on the link is often part of the same larger block the provider is about to delegate, and the provider needs the two to be combinable into a single route.

sections.title: The Solution: One Excluded Prefix
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new DHCPv6 option, OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE, code 67, used to exclude exactly one prefix from a delegated prefix. It is included in the OPTION_IAPREFIX IAprefix-options field, and there can be at most one such option in one OPTION_IAPREFIX option.

The arrangement it allows is that the requesting router is delegated a prefix, for example a /56, and the delegating router uses one prefix, for example a /64, on the link through which it exchanges DHCPv6 messages with the requesting router, taken from that same delegated set.

A requesting router includes the OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option code in an OPTION_ORO option in a Solicit, Request, Renew or Rebind message, to tell the delegating router that it supports the mechanism. A delegating router may include the same option code in an OPTION_ORO option in a Reconfigure message to ask the requesting router to request it.

The delegating router then includes in the OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option the prefix that is excluded from the delegated prefix set, and the requesting router MUST NOT assign the excluded prefix to any of its downstream interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage:
The new option sits inside the option that carries the delegated block, and it names exactly one prefix to hold back. The block that is delegated can be a /56, while the provider's own link to the customer router keeps a /64 taken from that same /56.

The customer router says in its request that it understands the option, so the provider only uses it with routers that can cope. The rule for the other side is simple: the prefix named in the option must not be used on any of the customer router's own downstream interfaces.

sections.title: How the Option Is Encoded
sections.content:
The option has four fields. The option code is OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE, 67. The option-len is 1 plus the length of the IPv6 subnet ID in octets, so a valid value is between 2 and 17. The prefix-len is the length of the excluded prefix in bits, and it MUST be between the OPTION_IAPREFIX prefix-length plus 1 and 128. The IPv6 subnet ID is a variable-length value of up to 128 bits.

The subnet ID carries only the bits that distinguish the excluded prefix from the delegated one: it holds prefix-len minus the OPTION_IAPREFIX prefix-length bits taken from the excluded prefix starting at bit position OPTION_IAPREFIX prefix-length. Those bits are then left-shifted so that they start on a full octet boundary, a shift of OPTION_IAPREFIX prefix-length modulo 8 bits, and the result is zero-padded to the next full octet boundary. The RFC gives the calculation as C-like pseudocode and also as a worked example: a router that was assigned 2001:db8:dead:beef::/64 while the delegated prefix is 2001:db8:dead:bee0::/59 encodes the excluded prefix with a prefix-len of 64 and a single octet of subnet ID, because the two prefixes differ in only a few bits.

Three rules apply to the option's placement and content. It MUST only be included in the OPTION_IAPREFIX IAprefix-options field. Any prefix excluded from the delegated prefix MUST be contained in an OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option within the corresponding OPTION_IAPREFIX. And the prefix in the option MUST be part of the delegated prefix in the OPTION_IAPREFIX; the excluded prefix also shares the same preferred-lifetime and valid-lifetime as the delegated prefix.
sections.plainLanguage:
The option is small. It has the usual code and length, then one byte giving the length in bits of the prefix being held back, then the bits that distinguish that prefix from the delegated one. Those bits are packed to the left so that they fill whole bytes, which saves space when the two prefixes are close together.

For example, a provider that delegates 2001:db8:dead:bee0::/59 and keeps 2001:db8:dead:beef::/64 for its own link needs only one byte to say so, because the two prefixes differ in a single bit position that the option can point at.

sections.title: Solicitation and Prefix Delegation
sections.content:
The requesting router finds and selects a delegating router in the same way as described in Section 11 of RFC 3633, and the RFC describes only the extra steps that the option requires.

On the requesting router side, if it implements the mechanism it SHOULD include the OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option code in the OPTION_ORO option of Solicit messages. On receiving the Advertise messages, it uses the prefixes received in OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE, in addition to the advertised prefixes, to choose the delegating router, and MUST then proceed with the prefix delegation procedure. If the Advertise message did not include the option, it MUST fall back to the normal behaviour of Section 11.1 of RFC 3633.

On the delegating router side, if the OPTION_ORO option in the Solicit includes the option code, the delegating router knows the requesting router supports the mechanism. If the Solicit also contains an IA_PD option, the delegating router can delegate a prefix that includes the prefix already assigned to the requesting router's uplink interface, and it includes that prefix in the OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option within the OPTION_IAPREFIX IAprefix-option of the Advertise message. If the OPTION_ORO does not include the option code, the delegating router MUST fall back to the normal behaviour of Section 11.2 of RFC 3633. If the option code is present but the delegating router does not support the mechanism, it acts as specified in RFC 3633.

The same steps apply to a requesting router initiated delegation, using a Request message instead of a Solicit. The requesting router returns the delegated prefixes with a Release message, and the prefixes to be released MUST be included in the IA_PDs along with the excluded prefix from the OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option. It MUST NOT use the option to introduce an additional excluded prefix in the Release message for which it originally got a valid binding. The requesting router must create sink routes for the delegated prefixes minus the excluded prefixes, which can be done by creating sink routes for the delegated prefixes and more specific routes for the excluded prefixes. On the delegating router side, the prefixes in a Release message may be marked as available, excluding the prefix in the OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE options. If the Release message contains a new excluded prefix in any OPTION_PD_EXCLUDE option, the delegating router MUST send a Reply message with the Status Code set to NoBinding for that IA_PD option.
sections.plainLanguage:
The exchange is an ordinary DHCPv6 one with one addition. The customer router lists the new option code among the options it asks for, and the provider, if it supports the mechanism, answers with the block of prefixes and names the one prefix it is keeping for the link.

If the provider's answer does not contain the option, the customer router goes back to the ordinary rules. If the customer router asks for an option the provider does not support, the provider simply behaves as before.

When the customer router later hands the prefixes back with a Release message, it must send the excluded prefix along with them, and it must not use the option to hold back a prefix it was never given. If it does, the provider answers with a Reply that says there is no such binding.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations for DHCPv6 are described in Section 23 of RFC 3315, and those for DHCPv6 prefix delegation in Section 15 of RFC 3633, which also gives recommendations for protection against prefix delegation attacks. This RFC adds no new security considerations beyond those provided by RFC 3633.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security rules. The rules that already apply to DHCPv6 and to prefix delegation apply here too, including the advice about defending against attacks that abuse prefix delegation.
